title: Spanish Filler Words: Pues, Bueno, O Sea and More

meta_description: Spanish filler words that make you sound natural: pues, bueno, este, o sea, a ver, la verdad, vale and en plan, with how and where each is used, plus a quiz.

body_html:
Spanish filler words are the small words that hold real conversations together: pues, bueno, o sea, a ver and, in Mexico, the famous este…. Textbooks rarely teach them, yet they are what make Spanish speakers sound relaxed and natural. For learners, they do something even more useful: they buy you a second to think without falling into silence or switching to English “um”. Here are the fillers you will hear most, what each one signals and where it is used.

Quick answer
  • Thinking time: este… (Mexico), eh…, a ver…, pues…
  • Starting or changing topic: bueno, mira, oye
  • Explaining: o sea, es que, la verdad
  • Spain: vale, en plan; Argentina: che, nada
{{toc}}

Spanish filler words for thinking time

WordMeaningExample
este…um… (Mexico)Quería, este… preguntarte algo. (I wanted to, um… ask you something.)
eh…uh…Eh… no sé. (Uh… I don’t know.)
a ver…let’s see…A ver… creo que es por aquí. (Let’s see… I think it’s this way.)
pues…well…Pues… no estoy seguro. (Well… I’m not sure.)
¿cómo se dice?how do you say it?Es un… ¿cómo se dice?… un destornillador. (It’s a… how do you say it?… a screwdriver.)
digamoslet’s sayLlegamos, digamos, a las ocho. (We arrive, let’s say, at eight.)

Replacing English “um” with este… or eh… is one of the quickest ways to sound less foreign. Native listeners hear an English “um” as a switch of language; a Spanish filler keeps you inside Spanish.

Starting, reacting and changing the subject

WordMeaningExample
buenowell, okayBueno, ¿empezamos? (Okay, shall we start?)
miralookMira, la verdad es que no puedo. (Look, the truth is I can’t.)
oyehey, listenOye, ¿tienes un minuto? (Hey, do you have a minute?)
¿sabes?you know?Es difícil, ¿sabes? (It’s hard, you know?)
¿no?right?Es mañana, ¿no? (It’s tomorrow, right?)
entoncessoEntonces, ¿qué hacemos? (So, what do we do?)
totalanyway, in the endTotal, que no fuimos. (Anyway, we didn’t go.)

In Mexico, bueno is also how many people answer the phone: ¿Bueno? See {{link:phone-calls-in-spanish|phone calls in Spanish}}.

{{image:2}}

Explaining and softening: o sea, es que, la verdad

  • O sea means “I mean” or “in other words”, and it introduces a clarification: Es caro, o sea, muy caro. (It’s expensive, I mean, really expensive.) Overused, it can sound like a teenager.
  • Es que introduces an excuse or explanation and softens a refusal: Es que mañana trabajo. (It’s just that I work tomorrow.)
  • La verdad means “honestly” or “to be honest”: La verdad, no me gustó. (Honestly, I didn’t like it.)
  • Tipo is used like “like” by younger speakers: Había, tipo, cien personas. (There were, like, a hundred people.)

Es que is especially useful for polite refusals; see {{link:disagreeing-politely-in-spanish|disagreeing politely in Spanish}}.

Regional fillers

FillersWhere you’ll hear them
este… / ¿mande? / óraleMexico
vale / en plan / ¿sabes?Spain
che / nada / visteArgentina
pues / ¿cierto? / ¿sí o qué?Colombia

In Argentina, nada is used to wrap up a story: Y nada, me fui a casa (And so, yeah, I went home). In Spain, en plan works like “like”. For more regional words, see {{link:mexican-slang|Mexican slang}}, {{link:spain-slang|Spain slang}} and {{link:argentine-slang|Argentine slang}}.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Fillers for reacting while you listen

Fillers aren’t only for speaking. Spanish speakers also use short reactions to show they are listening, and silence can feel cold. Try ajá (uh-huh), ya (I see, especially in Spain and Chile), claro (of course), ¿en serio? (really?), ¡qué bueno! (that’s great!) and ay, no (oh no). Dropping one in every few seconds while someone tells a story is a simple way to keep the conversation warm.

How to use filler words without overdoing them

Fillers are like salt: a little makes speech natural, too much spoils it. A few guidelines:

  1. Pick two or three that match the Spanish you hear most, for example este, bueno and o sea for Mexico.
  2. Use them at the start of a sentence to buy time, not in the middle of every phrase.
  3. Drop them in writing. They belong in speech and casual texts, not emails; see {{link:writing-emails-in-spanish|writing emails in Spanish}}.
  4. Listen first. Notice which fillers the people around you use, and copy them.

Linguists call these words discourse markers. The Instituto Cervantes’ Centro Virtual Cervantes includes material on how they work in Spanish conversation.

{{image:3}}

A sample conversation

Ana: Oye, ¿vienes a la cena el sábado?
Hey, are you coming to dinner on Saturday?

Mark: Este… la verdad, no sé. Es que tengo mucho trabajo.
Um… honestly, I don’t know. It’s just that I have a lot of work.

Ana: Bueno, pero es solo un rato, ¿no?
Well, it’s only for a little while, right?

Mark: A ver… o sea, sí, puedo ir un ratito. ¡Va!
Let’s see… I mean, yes, I can go for a bit. Okay!

Without the fillers, Mark’s answer would sound abrupt. With them, it sounds thoughtful and friendly. For more conversation strategies, see {{link:small-talk-in-spanish|small talk in Spanish}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Spanish filler words are small, but they change how you sound more than almost anything else. Choose a few that match the Spanish around you, use them to buy time, and you will feel less pressure in every conversation. For more natural expressions, see my guide to {{link:spanish-slang|Spanish slang}}.

faq.a: Small words like pues, bueno, este, o sea and a ver that speakers use to think, start a sentence, clarify or soften what they say.

faq.q: What do Mexicans say instead of “um”?
faq.a: Usually este…, and also eh… or mmm….
It means “I mean” or “in other words”.
Yes, a few. They make you sound natural and give you time to think. Just don’t overuse them.

questions.explain: Es que no puedo sounds softer than no puedo.

questions.q: La verdad at the start of a sentence means…

questions.explain: Leave them out of formal writing.
